title: Show HN: SimCity, but with Permits
titleZh: Show HN: SimCity, but with Permits
author: pcai
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Build the city of your dreams. Subject to approval You are the mayor. You know exactly what this city needs. Now get it past the zoning board, the neighbors, the appeals court and the next election. New game Free, because you are loved

Permit Pending is a city simulation in the spirit of the classics, with one difference: you are not a god. You are an elected mayor. Every apartment block, bus lane and factory goes through hearings, reviews, objections, lawsuits and appeals. The economy underneath is real. The neighbors are not always rational. Win the argument, or win the election. Ideally both.

How a good idea dies A typical case from your inbox. The economic answer was obvious. The political path was not. Month 1A tech boom pushes rents up. Young residents start to complain. Month 3You rezone an empty lot for a 12-story apartment building. Month 4Filed. Nearby homeowners organize over parking and "neighborhood character." Month 7Hearing. You trade height for parking. The building is now 6 stories. Month 8The smaller project no longer pays. The developer asks for a tax break. Month 9Housing advocates criticize the lower count of affordable units. Month 11Appeal. The board delays construction. A lawsuit is filed. Month 42Rents are still rising. Young voters blame you for the shortage. Homeowners blame you for the proposal. Month 48Election day.

Build absolutely nothing Every improvement creates opposition New housing lowers rents and angers homeowners. New industry brings jobs and smog. Better transit attracts development, and development attracts opponents. Fix one problem and you create a new group of voters who are angry about it. Hearings, appeals and lawsuits Your inbox fills with applications, controversies and recurring characters. Negotiate concessions at public hearings, win votes on a seven-seat council, and spend your political clout wisely. Some cases last longer than your term. An economy that keeps score Residents have ages, incomes and homes. Businesses hire, grow and leave. Land values, rents, jobs, taxes and services all connect. The city keeps changing while you are stuck in committee. Reelection every four years High-turnout groups have more power than their numbers suggest. Know who votes. Understand every failure Heatmaps, graphs and plain explanations show why voters are angry and which decision did it. The local paper The Gazette reports your successes, your scandals and your parking minimums. Sandbox forever No campaign and no win screen. The city goes on as long as the voters let you.
Pick your city Start with a hamlet at a crossroads, or inherit somebody else's problems.

comments.author: goda90
comments.textRawHtml: The various decisions/petitions that pop up can break the immersion by mentioning details that don't fit the city(petitions with signatures from >250% of the town population, traffic issues at the "4-way intersection in front of the feed store" when no such place exists, or the new building causing shadows when there's nothing around it). It would be great if more text was turned into templates that pull game data for accuracy, and if the simulation were able to feed definitive descriptions of the town layout into generative AI prompts to make the text talk about scenarios reflected in the game.

children.author: noduerme
children.textRawHtml:
I'm a huge fan of city builders and a politics nerd... I can't wait to try this. But I hope it really is procedural in the details too!

To the parent post: I have actually seen public interest groups bring petitions to a small city council with more signatures than there are residents of the city... but hopefully there's some countervailing force in this game too where local residents reject petitions that are driven by outside parties. In other words, not every signatory to a petition is a resident, and there's local resistance to regional causes. I guess this happens quite a bit more in the exurbs of major metropolitan areas.

children.author: rkagerer
children.textRawHtml:
First, it's awesome the developer is giving this away for free. I love the tongue in cheek approach, and the polish and labour-of-love artifacts visible in portions of the UI and gameplay.

That said, after playing it for a while something just felt "off". I like the idea of being involved in individual proposals, but there are too many immersion-breaking dialogs that come up (some of which just seem too irrelevant). And the text in them is sometimes "off" in a fashion that feels like it was written by AI (though I'm not sure if it was). The news articles and such in SimCity felt more hand-curated, concise and clever - thus more entertaining.

comments.author: blobbers
comments.textRawHtml:
I haven't tried the game, but this is slightly hilarious and awesome.

I've often wondered about this kind of thing. When I go to an airport, it seems strange to me that each one is different with some of them having elaborate train systems, or multiple runways.

The engineer in me says "surely there is an optimal solution, so why are they all so different?". Is there a simulator?

Sim City was a fantastic simulation from the stand point of a game, but I'm curious; if you build a city simulator and let it grow organically (game of life style) can you put in sufficient regulation/parameters that get you to where we are today?

And if so, is there a simulation that shows us a way to get us to a better tomorrow?

children.author: buildsjets
children.textRawHtml:
Every airport is different because every local geography, existing land use, and weather pattern is different.

Seattle has generally ether north or south winds depending on season, and the airport is located on the only buildable flat plateau for miles around, so has 3 runways all going the same direction, N/S.

https://wrcc-archive.dri.edu/cgi-bin/wea_windroseclim.pl?laK...

Denver built an all-new airport way outside of town where there was unlimited buildable land. Their winds are highly variable even within one season, so they have 6 runways in a crossing configuration.

https://wrcc-archive.dri.edu/cgi-bin/wea_windroseclim.pl?laK...

children.author: nkrisc
children.textRawHtml:
> The engineer in me says "surely there is an optimal solution, so why are they all so different?". Is there a simulator?

Optimistically, because each one has a different optimal solution given all the unique constraints for each airport project.

Also, airports aren't just built and then done. Often the cities around them will grow and the airports will need to expand and adapt to new constraints, sometimes many decades after they were first built.

children.author: dlcarrier
children.textRawHtml:
The optimal airport has two parallel runways, 9,000 feet apart, that align with prevailing wind. If a location has variable strong winds, another set can be built at a 90° angle. It's possible to add more runways at 9,000 intervals, but you're usually better off building an airport somewhere else.

Most airports were built during or before WWII, so few are designed to most efficiently accommodate modern usage. Maybe in the future we can better handle closer runways in low visibility, but first we'll have to figure out how to have two computers communicate directly with each other, instead of having one computer generate routes that get read out load by a human, transmitted over an analog radio, listened to by another human, then typed into another computer.

comments.author: zabriel_goss
comments.textRawHtml:
The original EPCOT as imagined by Walt Disney was a master-planned city, with all the pleasant amenities and cleverest design you could imagine in the 1960's: Walkable areas, clean public transit, no traffic congestion, homes furnished with the latest in technology and appliances. It was his greatest ambition at the end of his life to make it a reality.

But it didn't happen. Namely, because of how much central control would be given to one man and/or his company to pull it off. The plan in its early iterations essentially meant that if you lived in EPCOT, you forfeited certain freedoms, such as what goes in your home, where you worked, and so on.

This game gave me a good chuckle as a Sim City fan. I'm guilty of complaining about politicians of all levels. But I don't envy their position of having to cut through the vines of competing motives and regulations. And at the same time, as a citizen, I'm not sure I would opt for the Utopian alternative.
